Q: New WG21 paper P4043R0: Are C++ Contracts Ready to Ship in C++26? A:

Reading a bit more, I think I see a glaring hole wrt multi-threading. Say x and y are atomic<int>, then even [[pre(x.load(std::memory_order_acquire) < y..load(std::memory_order_acquire)] isn't one atomic operation and can lead to inconsistency (toctu like) issues. And this gets only worse when global variables/member variables are used within a contract. So in that respect using contracts may introduce a false sense of security in a multi-threaded environment and this is bound to cause issues in practice.

Reading further
I see this issue is kind of known/implied... and I would consider it a blocking issue for release.

Could be resolved by allowing (directly invoked?) lambdas
pre[[[]{std::scoped_lock mtx; return x < y; }]

Q: can u make an image diffuser in c? A:

Any Turing complete language can do anything.

But quite honestly, it sounds like you're not really ready do do "an image diffuser" in any language, not unless you find libraries that does all the work for you. Learn the basics, learn the theory, spend a few years studying, and you'll be ready. Or use existing pre-made solutions.

Also, asking for library recommendations, in questions or open-ended discussions, is not on topic here.

Q: Why does JSON not allow encoding infinities and NaN? A:

Douglas Crockford’s talk “JSON: The Fat-Free Alternative to XML”, as transcribed on JSON.org, gives this explanation:

A number can be represented as integer, real, or floating point. JSON does not support octal or hex because it is minimal. It does not have values for NaN or Infinity because it does not want to be tied to any particular internal representation.

This is a somewhat cryptic explanation. But I think an excerpt from another one of his talks, “The JSON Saga” can help interpret it:

JSON is the intersection […] of all modern programming languages. All languages have some sense of data, and structures of data. […] Every language expresses these differently, and will add a lot of other stuff on top of it, like type systems, and semantics. But they all have the same idea about what the data looks like, and JSON has the thing that's common to everything. By being at the intersection, it turns out to be the thing that everybody can agree on, so it's really easy to pass data back and forth. Prior data interchange formats tended to try to be the union of all the languages, and that turns out to be horrendously complex, and very difficult to deal with. JSON, by being so simple, actually became really easy to use.

So the desire was to only provide common, timeless data types and structures. And it seems like infinities and NaNs were deemed not timeless enough, too likely to cause interoperability problems, too much attached to the particulars of IEEE 754 to be worth including.

Ironically, most (schema-less) implementations of JSON do parse numbers into IEEE 754 doubles anyway, which enables representing infinity in JSON as, for example, 9e999, by counting on the recipient to round that to infinity upon parsing. But that’s likely to cause interoperability problems with implementations that, for once, do try to parse numbers of arbitrary precision losslessly; thus creating the very kind of encroachment of implementation details that Crockford seems to have wanted to avoid. If infinities were representable in JSON directly, this interoperability problem would not exist. (I could, however, defend omitting NaNs – null should probably suffice for the purpose of representing absent or invalid values.)
